headline: Ancient Peace Treaty Fragment Unearthed in Turkey
meta_description: Researchers in Turkey have discovered a clay tablet containing the world's oldest peace treaty, signed over 3,000 years ago between two ancient superpowers.
summary_short: A newly discovered clay tablet in Turkey contains sections of the Peace of Kadesh, the world's oldest known peace treaty between ancient Egypt and the Hittite kingdom.
body:
Archaeologists working at the ancient Hittite capital of Hattusa in central Turkey have uncovered a clay tablet inscribed with portions of the Peace of Kadesh—the world's oldest known peace treaty. The fragment, containing articles 12 through 20, was discovered during excavations at the royal palace at Buyukkale and represents a monumental step in understanding how ancient civilizations resolved their deepest conflicts. Written in Akkadian cuneiform, the tablet preserves pledges of eternal friendship, lasting peace, territorial integrity, and mutual defense between two ancient superpowers, language that echoes the ideals of modern international governance.

The Peace of Kadesh emerged from one of history's most significant military confrontations. Around 1,300 BCE, the armies of Egyptian pharaoh Ramses II collided with forces led by Hittite king Muwatallis II in what may have been the largest chariot battle ever recorded. Involving tens of thousands of soldiers, the clash ended in stalemate—neither side able to claim victory. Years later, Muwatallis' successor chose diplomacy over continued bloodshed, negotiating an agreement that would reshape relations between the two kingdoms.

What makes this discovery particularly remarkable is the treaty's humanitarian character. Beyond territorial and military provisions, the document established an extradition process with built-in amnesty protections—those returned to their home country faced no punishment such as home destruction, family seizure, or physical harm. This compassionate approach to conflict resolution stands as a sobering reminder of how much progress the world has made, and how much further it must go. The tablet's emergence offers hope that the impulse toward peace and understanding among human societies runs deep in our shared history.
quick_facts: Clay tablet found at Hattusa, Turkey contains world's oldest peace treaty
Signed around 1,300 BCE between Egypt's Ramses II and Hittite king Muwatallis II
Treaty pledged eternal friendship, lasting peace, and mutual defense
Tablet fragment contains articles 12–20 written in Akkadian cuneiform
Only 3 complete copies of this treaty are known to exist today
